Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-08 15:00 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Product), Aisha Rahman (Lighthouse Head Eng), Tom Alvarez (Platform), Priya Sharma (Security), Ben Ortiz (Frontend)

--- Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect) ---
Redwood gave an integration-focused demo oriented to an fintech customer's constraints: low-latency payments chat, need for private data controls, and predictable cost. Showed hosted API streaming behavior, param effects (max_tokens, temperature, top_p), and Console/Optimize guidance for batching and quantization recommendations. Next steps: security docs, pilot pricing, bench script.

00:00 Maya: Okay, hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Evan will do the deep technical bits; Jordan's here for product context. How's everyone doing?
00:12 Aisha: Good, thanks. Quick context: our team is building an in-app payments assistant, needs chat responses under 2s p95 and we process a lot of short prompts, about 40% are templated confirmations.
00:28 Tom: We also have strict data residency requirements for EU traffic and need audit logs surfaced to our SIEM.
00:35 Maya: Great, that's super helpful. I'll hand it to Evan to show a quick hosted demo and then we'll jump into Console and Optimize. Evan?
00:42 Evan: Thanks. Alright, I'm going to share my screen, show the hosted /chat endpoint behavior with streaming, and change params live. First note: streaming here is chunked; we flush partial tokens as they generate, so you can render progressively.
01:05 Evan: (on-screen) Example call: POST /v1/chat.generate with stream=true. You get SSE-ish framed events. If a client disconnects briefly we keep the KV cache warm for short windows but reconnect patterns matter.
01:21 Ben: Quick question — KV cache, is that per session or per model instance?
01:26 Evan: It's per request route + conversation key by default; short-term prefix caching is kept in the serving tier. That's, uh, why we sometimes talk about prefix or K-V cash in notes, soz — transcription artifacts.
01:40 Priya: On security: do you persist any prompt text in logs by default? We need to know retention policy and encryption.
01:47 Maya: Good call. By default hosted keeps request/response logs for 30 days for debug, but for enterprise pilots we can change retention and route logs to your SIEM, or disable logs. We'll include KMS support and field-level redaction patterns in the security pack.
02:05 Aisha: So for latency vs cost, what's the typical tradeoff? We want low-latency but also predictable cost for high QPS.
02:12 Evan: Right. Two levers: model choice + batching. For short prompts the per-token overhead dominates, so very small batching (micro-batching) can help throughput but add latency. We recommend reserved Dedicated pools for predictable latency at higher QPS. For hosted, Optimize will suggest batching and quantization profiles to hit your cost target.
02:35 Tom: You mentioned Dedicated — does that require extra network setup like VPC peering?
02:40 Evan: Dedicated can be configured with private egress and VPC peering or via a private endpoint depending on the region. We'll map that in the infra doc. For on-prem or air-gapped we have Redwood Private too, but that's a larger lift.
02:55 Maya: Jordan, can you show Console views for token breakdown and per-route latency?
03:01 Jordan: Yeah, switching to Console. Here is a route dashboard: avg token count, p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens. You'll also see a per-route model fallback history — if a model overloads we'll auto-route to a cheaper variant and log the event.
03:22 Evan: Important to call out — fallbacks are model-compatible variants; that means sometimes you get different quality, and you can set policy to prefer cost vs quality.
03:34 Ben: If we do fallbacks, can we get a diff or annotation so UX can show a degraded mode?
03:40 Jordan: Yes, Console marks fallback events, and we expose webhook events with reason codes so you can instrument UX changes.
03:48 Aisha: About retries: how should our client implement retries for stream disconnects? Do you recommend idempotency keys?
03:55 Evan: For short generative chat we recommend: 1) use idempotency keys for non-streamed calls to dedupe, 2) for streaming implement exponential backoff with jitter and resume by conversation id where possible; our SDKs include helpers. If you must retry the last token range we can advise on resume semantics, but sometimes it's better to treat a disconnect as transient and request a short regeneration.
04:23 Tom: Any best practices for parameter defaults? We've been tweaking temperature and top_p a lot.
04:28 Evan: Typical defaults: temperature=0.2 for deterministic UX, top_p=0.9 if you want diverse outputs, max_tokens sized to expected completion length; also set stop tokens to avoid over-generation in structured responses. Use n=1 unless you need multiple candidates — that's extra cost.
04:45 Maya: I'll jump in — Optimize can run a sweep over your prompt set and recommend both model family and tokenization/quantization profiles, shows estimated cost delta and expected latency impact. It's a guided recommendation; you can preview suggestions in Console.
04:59 Priya: Does Optimize share quantization details that would affect confidentiality? Are model weights exposed?
05:05 Jordan: No, Optimize's recommendations are operational — e.g., use a 4-bit quantized variant of model X; we don't expose weights. We document the tradeoffs: sometimes 4-bit reduces quality slightly; we tie regressions to your eval set.
05:20 Aisha: Hmm, we have many templated prompts — can we exploit prefix caching to reduce tail latency?
05:26 Evan: Yes, if you have repeated prefixes we can cache the KV state for those prefixes and warm the service; Console will show hit rates. Caveat: caching is most effective when prompts are identical or near-identical.
05:40 Ben: On the dev side, how do we simulate production load?
05:44 Evan: We'll provide a bench script; it's a simple harness that replays your sample prompts at chosen concurrency with token accounting. I'll attach the script to the follow-up.
05:53 Aisha: Security deep dive — Priya, any questions for Redwood?
05:56 Priya: KMS integration: do you support customer-managed keys, and HSM? Also SSO mapping and RBAC for console access.
06:05 Maya: Yes to CMKs via KMS in supported clouds, HSM options for Private deployments. SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning are supported for enterprise accounts; RBAC is role-based in Console. We'll include screenshots in the security pack.
06:20 Priya: And audit logs can be forwarded to our Splunk?
06:23 Jordan: Yes, log forwarding to your SIEM is standard for enterprise pilots. We can also provide immutable audit trails for-specific routes if needed.
06:35 Tom: Let's talk about failure modes — e.g., model OOMs or sudden latency spikes. How does Redwood fail gracefully?
06:42 Evan: Several layers: autoscaling (for Dedicated), model fallbacks, and cross-region failover. For hosted we have tiers: primary model, cheaper fallback, and last-resort short-text model. Console shows fallback counts and we can set auto-rollbacks if regressions exceed thresholds.
06:58 Aisha: Any example SLO we can reasonably aim for on hosted?
07:02 Maya: For small-ish workloads hosted can hit ~1s p50 and 2-3s p95 on low-latency models; but p95 is sensitive to sequence length and burstiness. Dedicated gives tighter SLOs. We'll capture expected p95 ranges in the benchmark report.
07:20 Ben: Do you support streaming with chunked structured events? We need JSON chunks to update the UI progressively.
07:27 Evan: Yes, you can stream structured deltas; we have an events format where each chunk includes a type field and delta content. Be careful with partial JSON — we recommend sending small newline-delimited protocol buffers or framing to avoid parse errors on the client.
07:49 Maya: I'm going to demo a quick live call. We'll show a normal stream, then induce a reconnect to show resume semantics.
08:00 Evan: (demo) Starting chat, stream opens, tokens flow, UI receives progressive text. Now I simulate a disconnect — client reconnects with same conversation id — we can resume but some state may need regeneration.
08:28 Ben: That interruption looked like duplicate tokens sometimes. How to avoid duplication on resume?
08:33 Evan: Use sequence offsets we include in each chunk; client should track last offset and request resume from offset+1. SDKs hide that complexity, but it's important for custom clients.
08:46 Tom: Regarding quotas and rate limits — how do you surface throttling?
08:50 Jordan: Console shows per-API key rate limits and historical throttles. For hosted we have soft quotas and burst buffers. For enterprise pilots we typically tune rate limits and can provide dedicated pools to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
09:07 Aisha: For our payment confirmations we need deterministic wording. How do we guard against hallucinations?
09:12 Evan: Use a mix of tactics: 1) tight sampling params (low temp), 2) constrained prompts/templates with stop tokens, 3) a validation reranker or a structured response schema (e.g., JSON) with strict parsing and an acceptance filter. We also recommend a lightweight post-check step or a verification API that validates critical fields.
09:38 Ben: Could Redwood do a rerank on-device or is that an extra API call?
09:43 Evan: Reranking is an extra step in the flow — you can do it with a cheaper model or an embedding-based reranker. Optimize can recommend a rerank setup that balances cost.
09:52 Maya: We're getting some questions about observability: what traces and token-level breakdowns are available?
09:58 Jordan: We emit trace hooks and per-token timing; Console surfaces tokenization time vs model compute vs network. You can export traces to your tracing backend.
10:10 Tom: For EU data, can you keep EU traffic in EU-only regions?
10:13 Maya: Yes, region pinning and data residency options exist for enterprise subscriptions. For hosted we have region endpoints and for Dedicated you can reserve capacity in target regions.
10:24 Aisha: On the topic of cost, can we set policy to prefer cost-optimized model for non-critical flows?
10:30 Jordan: Absolutely — routing policies allow you to tag routes as critical vs non-critical and auto-route non-critical to cheaper variants during peak. Console will show cost impact.
10:40 Evan: Quick note on quantization: using a 4-bit variant can drop latency significantly, but sometimes increases small-scope hallucinations; we always recommend A/B tests against your eval set. Optimize automates that A/B and reports quality regressions.
10:58 Maya: Let's do a rapid Q&A from the customer.
11:02 Aisha: If we hit 2k RPS for a burst, what's the recommended architecture?
11:07 Evan: For bursts at that scale you want Dedicated or a hybrid: reserve base Dedicated capacity and fall back to hosted elastic burst. Also use prefix caching and pre-warmed model workers for known peak windows.
11:22 Tom: How do you handle model upgrades? We can't have silent regressions.
11:27 Maya: We support pinned model versions and controlled rollouts — canary, A/B, and automatic rollback on eval regressions. Console exposes diff metrics and you'll get alerts if quality or latency drifts.
11:40 Priya: For compliance audits we need a package of logs and config history — is that exportable?
11:45 Jordan: Yes, audit exports with change history and user actions are available for enterprise. We'll attach sample export formats in the pack.
11:55 Ben: SDK language support? Our front-end is JS and backend is Go.
11:58 Evan: Official SDKs for JS, Python, Go are available; we also have lightweight REST examples.
12:06 Aisha: Any limitations on attachments or multimodal?
12:09 Evan: Hosted chat right now focuses on text and structured outputs. Image/multimodal is on the roadmap with separate model endpoints.
12:17 Maya: I'm going to show Optimize's recommendation flow quickly — upload a small eval set, run a sweep, Optimize suggests a quantized variant and batching config with estimated cost savings.
12:30 Jordan: (on-screen) Here you can click 'Preview diffs' — it runs synthetic replays and attaches quality deltas. You can accept or schedule a canary rollout.
12:46 Aisha: That preview is helpful. If we accept a quantize suggestion, can we limit it to a single route?
12:50 Jordan: Yes, suggestions are per-route and per-model; you can apply them selectively.
12:56 Tom: For the pilot, what's the timeline? We want a test in two weeks.
12:59 Maya: We can aim for a POC kickoff in the week of 2026-01-19 if you share sample prompts and traffic by 2026-01-12. We'll run bench and provide SLA targets.
13:12 Ben: Any gotchas with idempotency if we process payments and then confirm?
13:16 Evan: Ensure you use idempotency for actions that mutate payments. For generation calls that produce confirmations, have an atomic commit step to your payment system and log the generation id. Avoid double-charges by coupling generation id with transaction id.
13:30 Priya: Is there a SOC2 type 2 report we can review?
13:33 Maya: Yes, we'll include SOC2 Type II in the security pack; also list data flows and retention controls.
13:42 Aisha: Will Redwood host the bench infra or do we run it?
13:45 Evan: We'll provide a bench harness; you can run it in your environment against our sandbox endpoints or we can run it for you with anonymized samples.
13:56 Tom: Ok, last set: do you support custom model fine-tuning with private data?
14:00 Jordan: We support private model variants via Private deployments or Managed fine-tune for enterprise; hosted fine-tune options are limited due to data governance. We'll cover options in the follow-up.
14:12 Maya: Great, that wraps the demo. Quick recap: we'll send security pack, pricing and pilot scope by 2026-01-10; Evan will prepare bench script and initial benchmark targets; Lighthouse to provide prompts and infra diagram by 2026-01-12.
14:30 Aisha: Sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
14:35 Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up.

--- End meeting ---

Notes about transcription quality: system mislabels sometimes, proper nouns like KV cache occasionally transcribed oddly, and timestamps are approximate.
